mission.title: Mission
mission.text: The Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB) is an independent center for the generation, use, and transfer of knowledge based on research and critical analysis of biomedical research. Our main goal is to provide data, trends, patterns, and diagnostics on the quality of methods, principles, and foresight of scientific activity.

ivan.title: CEO & Founder CECIMIB SAS (Colombia)
ivan.detailed_bio:
Ivan David Lozada-Martinez is a medical researcher and full-time professor at the Universidad de la Costa (Barranquilla, Colombia), where he conducts research at the intersection of meta-science, scientometrics, evidence-based research, knowledge gaps in medical sciences, evidence-based medicine, global health, and geroscience. Throughout his career, he has been characterized by addressing questions of high translational impact: how biomedical evidence is produced, evaluated, and improved, and how that knowledge can be converted into more precise decisions in clinical practice, policies, and health systems.

On an institutional and scientific leadership level, he is the Leader of the Biomedical Scientometrics and Evidence-Based Research Unit (METRIC-BIO) in his academic department, and also serves as Scientific Director of the CECIMIB research group (Center for Meta-Research and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences; Barranquilla), an initiative aimed at strengthening reproducible research, critical evaluation, and responsible metrics in health.

One of his most visible lines of work focuses on extreme longevity and healthy aging, with an emphasis on research on centenarians in Colombia. Within the context of the Colombia Centenarians Project/Alliance, he has contributed to characterizing centenarian populations and discussing their epidemiological and translational implications.

In parallel, his production includes contributions to international journals and forums where he poses scientific questions combining demographics, public health, and geroscience, such as the discussion on under-registration or missing centenarians as a problem with global implications, as well as work on the conceptualization of blue zones and their utility for guiding healthy aging research and policies.

Another cross-cutting line in his work is meta-research applied to biomedical sciences: evaluating methodological quality, bias, transparency, incentives, and knowledge gaps, with explicit calls to strengthen these approaches in specific areas (e.g., neurosciences), and to consolidate capacities in low- and middle-income contexts.

His scientific and academic agenda converges on one goal: to produce and use better evidence so that biomedical knowledge is more rigorous, useful, and equitable, connecting quantitative analysis of research (scientometrics/meta-science) with clinical and population problems (geroscience, public health, global health). His public projections are oriented towards expanding research platforms and initiatives, consolidating interdisciplinary collaborations, and continuing to develop projects that bring high-quality evidence closer to decision-making in health.

david.title: Research Assistant
david.detailed_bio: David A. Hernandez-Paez is a physician-in-training, associate researcher at the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences, and a member of the International Biometric Society. His academic activity focuses on meta-research and the assessment of scientific production coherence by estimating its potential impact on population indicators and health outcomes. His methodology utilizes regression models, hierarchical mixed-effects models, and moderator analysis. In 2025, he was awarded the Best Physician-in-Training Researcher in Colombia prize by the Association of Medical Student Scientific Societies of Colombia (ASCEMCOL).

andy.title: Research Assistant
andy.detailed_bio:
Andy A. Acosta-Monterrosa is a biologist from the University of Cartagena, research assistant at the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences, and member of the Colombian Association of Human Genetics and the Functional Diversity Research Network. His work integrates research in natural and biomedical sciences with a strong quantitative component, focusing on data management, analysis, and visualization, and biostatistics in R, in addition to scientific dissemination and communication.

His academic activity is organized into two axes; marine biodiversity of the Colombian Caribbean, with an emphasis on ecology, diversity and taxonomy of macroalgae, marine conservation and coastal governance; and bibliometrics and meta-research, studying scientific production, research coherence and global patterns in health and the environment.

Complementarily, he has developed research in pharmacogenomics and genetic ancestry in Colombian populations, exploring how differences in the frequency of genetic variants can be related to variation in response to medications and the implementation of precision medicine approaches.

1-1-2026.title: Congratulations to Dr. Fabriccio J. Visconti-Lopez on Achieving the Category of Distinguished Researcher RENACYT
1-1-2026.author: Andy A. Acosta-Monterrosa
1-1-2026.subtitle: Recognition of scientific excellence and rigor in Peru.
1-1-2026.p1: The Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB) expresses its congratulations to Dr. Fabriccio J. Visconti-Lopez, international collaborator and academic affiliated with our research group, for having achieved the category of Distinguished Researcher RENACYT, the highest classification granted by the National Council of Science, Technology and Technological Innovation, CONCYTEC, of Peru.
1-1-2026.p2: This recognition represents an important milestone in his career as a researcher and reflects his scientific production, academic commitment, methodological rigor, and contribution to the development of biomedical research, public health, and meta-research.
1-1-2026.p3: From CECIMIB, we highlight this achievement with special satisfaction, since approximately only 2% of the registered researchers in Peru obtain this distinction. This reaffirms the importance of promoting quality scientific research, with academic impact and oriented to answer relevant questions for health and society.
1-1-2026.p4: We commend Dr. Visconti-Lopez for this national recognition and express our gratitude to him for being part of our academic community. His trajectory constitutes an example of perseverance, discipline, and commitment to science.
1-1-2026.p5: Dr. Visconti-Lopez is an active contributor in the research lines of meta-science, evidence-based medicine, biomedical scientometrics, epidemiology, and global health.

1-2-2026.p2: This important international achievement highlights her scientific trajectory, academic leadership, and commitment to the transformation of health systems through research, innovation, and emerging technologies applied to patient safety and quality of care. Her work in artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and 4.0 technologies reflects the impact that nursing can generate in strengthening public health and risk management in national and international contexts.
1-2-2026.p3: For CECIMIB, it is a matter of pride to have a professional whose trajectory represents excellence, discipline, and the generation of knowledge with social impact, contributing to the positioning of Latin American research in high-level global scenarios.
1-2-2026.p4: In our corporation, Johana Galván contributes to the lines of innovation and development in health, digital health, management of research and development projects, and public health.

1-4-2026.title: Does publishing more science mean improving people's lives?
1-4-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
1-4-2026.p1: Every year, millions of scientific articles are published worldwide. We are talking about new treatments, innovative technologies, artificial intelligence, vaccines, rare diseases, and hundreds of other topics. Science has never produced as much knowledge as it does now.
1-4-2026.p2: But there is a surprisingly simple question that for many years no one could clearly answer: Is all this research really helping to improve people's lives?
1-4-2026.p3: Although it may seem strange, the answer is not so obvious. For decades we have learned to measure how many articles a country publishes, how many times they are cited by other researchers, or in which journals they appear. These measurements are important because they allow us to understand scientific productivity. However, they all have one thing in common: they describe science from the inside.
1-4-2026.p4: What we rarely ask is whether this enormous scientific effort is truly aligned with the problems of society.
1-4-2026.p5: Imagine a city where more hospitals are built every year, but people continue to get sick from the same causes. No one would say that building hospitals is bad, but it would be reasonable to ask whether those hospitals are responding to the true needs of the population.
1-4-2026.p6: Something similar happens with scientific research. Publishing more does not guarantee, by itself, that diseases will decrease, treatments will improve, or public policies will be more effective. Precisely this was the question that motivated the approach of scientific coherence and development coherence.
1-4-2026.p7: Until now, there was no method specifically designed to study whether scientific production and health or development indicators evolved coherently over time. Most available tools evaluated the quality of publications, their academic impact, or the number of citations received, but very few analyzed the relationship between research and what happens in people's real lives.
1-4-2026.p8: To attempt to fill that gap, the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), developed a new methodological framework called DAIL, whose name comes from Data-driven Analysis and Inference of Longitudinal Population Indicators and Research Production.
1-4-2026.p9: Its purpose is not to say whether a research is good or bad. Its objective is much more ambitious; to estimate whether the growth of research on a topic seems to be accompanied by changes in indicators related to that same problem, and also to study how social, economic, or institutional conditions can influence a country's ability to produce science.
1-4-2026.p10: To understand it, an analogy may serve. Think of a doctor observing a patient's progress over several years. It is not enough to know how many medications the patient received; the doctor needs to compare that information with changes in blood pressure, weight, quality of life, and other indicators. Only then can they understand if there is a relationship between the treatment and the patient's progress.
1-4-2026.p11: DAIL applies a similar logic, but on a much larger scale. Instead of following a person, it analyzes countries, regions, or groups of countries over long periods. Instead of studying medications, it analyzes thousands of scientific publications. And instead of measuring only academic production, it compares it with health, development, education, or economic indicators available in international databases.
1-4-2026.p12: It is important to clarify something fundamental. This method does not demonstrate that research directly causes the observed changes. Reality is much more complex. The results allow identifying patterns of association and coherence, but always recognizing that there are many other factors that also influence and that causality cannot be established with this type of analysis. This methodological prudence is an essential part of the method itself.
1-4-2026.p13: Why does this matter for society, academia, and decision-making in research policies? If we learn to measure how aligned research is with the needs of the population, we can identify areas where science is generating a positive impact, but also those where there is an enormous research effort without yet reflecting benefits for society. This information can help guide future research, support decision-making, and strengthen evidence-based scientific policies.
1-4-2026.p14: Science has always sought to answer questions about the phenomena of nature. However, perhaps the time has come to ask a different question: how well is science itself responding to people's needs?
1-4-2026.p15: Answering that question does not only imply producing more knowledge. It implies learning to evaluate whether that knowledge advances coherently with the health, well-being, and development of societies. That was the reason that drove the construction of the DAIL method and, probably, one of the tools that seeks to contribute to the relevance and pertinence of scientific and academic activity in the 21st century.
1-4-2026.reference: Hernandez-Paez DA, Visconti-Lopez FJ, Lozada-Martınez ID. Estimating scientific coherence using population-level indicators and research production data: a longitudinal analytical proof-of-concept study. Front Res Metr Anal. 2026 Jun 29;11:1817595.
1-4-2026.caption: Scientific coherence study published in Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics for global development.

1-5-2026.title: Does researching a disease guarantee that it stops affecting people?
1-5-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
1-5-2026.p1: Every year, millions of people get sick from causes that most of the world never mentions. They do not frequently appear on the news, they rarely occupy the front pages of newspapers, and for many people, even their names are unknown. These are the so-called neglected tropical diseases.
1-5-2026.p2: Despite affecting more than a billion people, these diseases tend to concentrate in communities with high levels of poverty, limited access to health services, and few development opportunities. Over the past decades, the scientific community has devoted increasing efforts to studying them. Thousands of articles have been published, new projects developed, and international collaborations strengthened. But a question arose that seemed as simple as it was uncomfortable:
1-5-2026.p3: Is all this research really reaching those who need it most?
1-5-2026.p4: Answering that question was the purpose of a recently published study. To do so, the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), developed a study that included more than 107,000 research articles published over 25 years and compared them with international health indicators, such as the incidence of malaria, tuberculosis, HIV, and other neglected tropical diseases in different regions of the world.
1-5-2026.p5: This analysis did not seek to prove that research directly caused an improvement in health, because reality is much more complex. It aimed to explore whether both seemed to advance in the same direction, that is, if there was coherence between the knowledge that science produces and what happens to the health of populations.
1-5-2026.p6: The results were encouraging, but they also left important lessons. It was identified that, in several cases, a higher volume of research was associated with reductions in indicators related to HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, and some tropical diseases. However, this relationship did not appear in all indicators nor in all regions of the world. In some places, research seemed to advance much faster than the benefits observed in the population.
1-5-2026.p7: Why does this happen? Because publishing a scientific article is just the beginning of the road.
1-5-2026.p8: For a discovery to change a person's life, it must be transformed into public policies, prevention programs, available medications, trained professionals, and health systems capable of bringing that knowledge to communities. If any of those steps fail, even the best research can take many years to produce real benefits.
1-5-2026.p9: We can imagine it as a relay race. The researcher passes the baton to those who design health policies, then to those who organize health services, and finally to the professionals who care for patients. If any of those batons are dropped, knowledge never reaches the finish line. That was probably the most important lesson from our study.
1-5-2026.p10: It is not enough to produce more science. We must also ask whether that science is responding to people's needs and whether the conditions exist to turn knowledge into concrete actions. Research should not be evaluated solely by the number of articles published, but also by its capacity to contribute to solving the problems it attempts to study.
1-5-2026.p11: Neglected tropical diseases are named so because, for a long time, they were also neglected by research, funding, and public policies. Today we know that scientific production is growing and that this growth is already beginning to be reflected in some health indicators. However, this research shows that there is still a long way to go for this knowledge to equitably benefit all populations.
1-5-2026.p12: The true success of science is not measured solely by the articles it publishes, but by the lives it manages to transform.
1-5-2026.reference: Hernandez-Paez DA, Montoya-Quintero KF, Vidal-Durango JV, Lozada-Martínez ID. Measuring scientific coherence between global neglected tropical disease research and population health indicators: a 25-year meta-research study. Front Res Metr Anal. 2026 Jun 18;11:1766718.
1-5-2026.caption: Scientific coherence study published in Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics for tropical diseases.

1-6-2026.title: Can research on neglected tropical diseases transform more than just health?
1-6-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
1-6-2026.p1: When we think of research on neglected tropical diseases, it is common to imagine new medications, vaccines, or diagnostic tests. However, these diseases do not depend solely on medical advances. They are also closely related to access to clean water, sanitation, hygiene, the strength of health systems, and the ability of countries to generate their own scientific knowledge.
1-6-2026.p2: This raises a rare but fundamental question: can scientific research on neglected tropical diseases contribute to transforming these conditions, in addition to improving health?
1-6-2026.p3: Based on this question, the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), analyzed more than one hundred thousand research articles published over the past two decades and linked them with international indicators on access to health services, research investment, clean water, sanitation, and hygiene. Furthermore, they compared the results among high, middle, and low-income countries to understand whether the potential benefits of research were similar in different socioeconomic contexts.
1-6-2026.p4: The results showed a complex reality. In general terms, the researchers found that scientific activity does seem to be associated with improvements in some key indicators, but those benefits are not evenly distributed. That is, producing more knowledge does not guarantee that all countries obtain the same advantages.
1-6-2026.p5: The most consistent findings appeared in indicators related to water, sanitation, and hygiene, internationally known as WASH. It was observed that a higher volume of research was associated with a decrease in open defecation practices and a reduction in deaths related to unsafe sanitary conditions. Most interestingly, these associations were more pronounced in low-income countries, precisely where neglected tropical diseases represent a greater burden on the population.
1-6-2026.p6: They also identified positive associations with greater access to safely managed drinking water and, in some groups of countries, with better handwashing facilities. This suggests that research can contribute, indirectly, to strengthening essential environmental conditions to prevent the transmission of many of these diseases.
1-6-2026.p7: However, not all areas showed the same behavior. When scientific capacity and technological development were analyzed, important differences were found among country groups. In high-income nations, a greater availability of health research institutions was related to an increase in scientific production. Conversely, in several middle and low-income countries, that relationship was much more limited or even negative. Likewise, funding specifically destined for research on neglected tropical diseases produced different effects depending on each country's income level, demonstrating that investing resources does not always generate the same results in all contexts.
1-6-2026.p8: Results related to the state of health systems were also discovered. Scientific activity was associated with a reduction in out-of-pocket spending for accessing health services, especially in low and lower-middle-income countries. This finding suggests that scientific knowledge could contribute to more efficient health systems when conditions exist to incorporate evidence into decision-making.
1-6-2026.p9: Perhaps the most important lesson from this study is that research does not act only within hospitals or laboratories. Its effects can extend to much broader aspects, such as sanitation conditions, access to safe water, the organization of health systems, or a country's ability to generate innovation.
1-6-2026.p10: Neglected tropical diseases are, in essence, diseases deeply linked to social inequalities. Therefore, fighting them requires much more than developing new treatments. It also requires strengthening the conditions that allow preventing them, controlling them, and generating solutions from their own territories. Scientific research can be an engine of that change, but only when it is accompanied by public policies, sustained investment, and a real commitment to equity.
1-6-2026.reference: Hernandez-Paez DA, Lozada-Martinez ID, Reyes-Duque JD, Kalokoh S. Estimating the potential impact of global research on neglected tropical diseases on population-level indicators of health access, sanitation, and research capacity. PLoS Negl Trop Dis. 2026 May 21;20(5):e0014343.
1-6-2026.caption: Research impact study published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases for sanitation indicators.

2-4-2026.title: Is there an integrity crisis in global neurosurgery?
2-4-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
2-4-2026.p1: Neurosurgery is one of the most demanding medical specialties, not only due to the technical precision required in the operating room, but also because of the constant need for rigorous and reliable scientific evidence to make critical decisions. In this context, the integrity of scientific publications is fundamental.
2-4-2026.p2: However, a recent study has shed light on a concerning reality. Researchers from the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), along with its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), published a comprehensive analysis in the journal World Neurosurgery, evaluating hundreds of neurosurgery articles that had to be retracted—that is, withdrawn from journals—over nearly a quarter of a century, between 2000 and 2024.
2-4-2026.p3: The findings reveal a growing problem. Although the overall percentage of retracted articles may seem low, the authors demonstrated that the frequency of retractions increased significantly over time, with a particularly pronounced spike during the COVID-19 pandemic. This finding suggests that, under pressure, some editorial quality control systems may have been compromised, allowing the publication of studies with methodological flaws or, even worse, ethical irregularities.
2-4-2026.p4: The most alarming aspect of the study was the reasons that led to the withdrawal of these articles. The main documented cause was the systematic manipulation of the peer review process and the fraudulent use of "paper mills" to falsify audits. That is, some authors created fake reviewers or paid to guarantee favorable opinions about their own studies.
2-4-2026.p5: In addition to fraudulent review, plagiarism and duplication of previous research figured as frequent reasons for retraction. These behaviors not only violate basic ethical research norms but also contaminate the medical literature with evidence that could be false or misleading.
2-4-2026.p6: The study also highlighted marked regional differences. Institutions located in East Asia and the Pacific accounted for the largest number of retracted articles, followed by North America. This does not necessarily mean that more fraud is committed in these regions, but rather that surveillance systems, editorial policies, and institutional evaluation criteria likely vary significantly.
2-4-2026.p7: On the other hand, although a large part of the retracted research corresponded to basic sciences and laboratory trials, a considerable number of observational studies and even clinical trials were also identified. When a clinical trial is based on dubious data, the risk ceases to be solely academic and becomes a direct threat to patient safety and treatment.
2-4-2026.p8: Another critical aspect revealed by the analysis was that, on average, approximately one year and nine months elapsed from the time the articles were published until they were finally withdrawn. During all that time, these studies were available, could be read by medical professionals, and potentially used to guide subsequent research or clinical decisions.
2-4-2026.p9: Despite all of the above, not everything was negative. The study highlighted the fundamental role of tools such as the Retraction Watch database, which has allowed this information to be documented and organized, facilitating the identification and analysis of the problem globally.
2-4-2026.p10: In conclusion, the panorama described by this CECIMIB and METRIC-BIO study demands deep reflection on the incentives within the academic and scientific community. When the main goal is to "publish or perish", an environment conducive to questionable behaviors is created. Ensuring that neurosurgery continues to advance safely and reliably will require not only strengthening editorial review processes but also promoting a culture of integrity, transparency, and scientific rigor from the institutions that generate the evidence.
2-4-2026.caption: Scientific audit study published in Revista da Associação Médica Brasileira for the neurosurgery field.
2-4-2026.reference: Lozada-Martinez ID, Arias LMD, López JEM. Thousands of articles on neurosurgery, yet few self-assessments of neurosurgical evidence: the need to integrate meta-research for a more reliable clinical practice. Rev Assoc Med Bras (1992). 2026 May 11;72(2):e20251867.

2-5-2026.title: Does publishing more science on food security improve population food indicators?
2-5-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
2-5-2026.p1: The world faces a colossal challenge: ensuring that everyone has access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food. To achieve this, science plays a fundamental role. It is assumed that researching more about food security will generate the knowledge needed to improve nutrition and the living conditions of the population.
2-5-2026.p2: But does this really happen? Is there a direct connection between the number of studies published and real improvements in social indicators of food and health?
2-5-2026.p3: To answer this question, the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS) and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), analyzed a quarter of a century of global scientific research on food security (2000-2025). Their goal was to evaluate whether the increase in scientific publications was associated, in real life, with improvements in key indicators such as the prevalence of undernourishment, food insecurity, obesity, child malnutrition, and mortality from nutritional causes.
2-5-2026.p4: The findings revealed a fascinating landscape, but one that is also full of nuances. In general terms, the research showed that there is indeed a relationship between scientific activity and social improvements, but this connection depends largely on the income level of each country.
2-5-2026.p5: In high-income nations, a greater number of scientific publications seemed to be favorably associated with a better overall environment, reflected in variables such as life expectancy, government quality, institutional development, and even performance against climate change. In these countries, science seems to integrate more efficiently with other areas of development.
2-5-2026.p6: However, when specifically analyzing food problems in lower-income countries—where the burden of food insecurity is much higher—the results showed important challenges. The study found that, although the volume of research is positively related to some indicators (such as the reduction of stunting in children), that association is often lost or reversed when favorable institutional conditions do not exist.
2-5-2026.p7: One of the most interesting discoveries occurred when analyzing the "rule of law" and the control of corruption. The study demonstrated that the positive effect of food security research (such as reducing the prevalence of undernourishment or low birth weight) can be deeply nullified or weakened in environments with high corruption or institutional weakness.
2-5-2026.p8: In contrast, when countries have a solid rule of law, good territorial control, and more structured health systems, scientific research manages to enhance its benefits. In those favorable scenarios, knowledge seems to flow better from academic journals to public policies and, finally, to communities.
2-5-2026.p9: This finding changes the way we understand the role of research. For a long time, it has been assumed that producing more knowledge would automatically lead to better social outcomes. However, this study demonstrates that research is only part of the solution. If a country lacks institutions capable of transforming that knowledge into programs, policies, and interventions, even the best scientific evidence will have a limited impact.
2-5-2026.p10: The main message of this analysis is perhaps that fighting hunger requires much more than generating new scientific publications. It also requires strengthening the systems that allow that knowledge to reach the people. Research remains indispensable, but its true value depends not only on how many articles are published, but on the ability of each society to translate evidence into decisions that improve the food, nutrition, and quality of life of its population.
2-5-2026.caption: Scientific coherence study published in Global Food Security for food indicators.
2-5-2026.reference: Hernández-Paez DA, Vergara-Rios JC, Montoya-Quintero KF, Lozada-Martinez ID. Does food security research really improve people's lives? A framework to estimate its potential impact from 2000 to 2025. Global Food Security. 2026; 49:100925.

2-6-2026.title: Does greater scientific activity contribute to generating more food? Global evidence says not always
2-6-2026.author: Ivan D. Lozada Martínez
2-6-2026.p1: When we think of agriculture, we usually imagine improved seeds, fertilizers, machinery, or new technologies. We also tend to believe that if a country produces more scientific research on food and agriculture, it will inevitably end up producing more food.
2-6-2026.p2: But reality is much more complex. With the goal of answering this question, researchers from the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), analyzed global scientific production related to food security over the last 25 years, and compared it with the agricultural production of 23 different crops in countries of all income levels. In total, the study integrated more than 60,000 scientific articles along with international indicators of agricultural production and multiple variables related to governance, institutional capacity, health systems, and international financing.
2-6-2026.p3: The results question a widespread idea. Although initially there seemed to be many associations between the number of publications and agricultural production, most disappeared when researchers applied more rigorous statistical models that took into account differences between countries, changes over time, and the risk of obtaining falsely positive results. Of the 67 initially significant associations, only five remained robust after multivariate analysis.
2-6-2026.p4: This means that producing more scientific knowledge does not guarantee, by itself, greater food production. In fact, many crops showed negative associations. In cereals such as wheat, barley, maize, and rice, the increase in publications was related to reductions in production when certain economic contexts were analyzed. Something similar occurred with several horticultural products, such as potatoes and tomatoes. However, other crops, such as soybeans, sesame, bananas, or cocoa, showed completely different behaviors depending on each country's income level.
2-6-2026.p5: So why does this happen? Because research does not act in isolation. The study found that the real differentiating factor is the structural capacity of each country. Variables such as effective control of the territory, quality of government, levels of corruption, healthy life expectancy, access to health services, availability of researchers, and certain international cooperation mechanisms profoundly modify the relationship between research and agricultural production.
2-6-2026.p6: An example is especially illustrative. In countries with greater institutional control of the territory, the relationship between research and banana production changed completely: an initially negative association ended up becoming a positive association. The same occurred with crops like wheat and potatoes, where better governance significantly reduced the negative effect observed in countries with weaker institutions.
2-6-2026.p7: Something similar happened with scientific capacity and health systems. Countries with more researchers, better access to health services, and higher healthy life expectancy showed a greater capacity to transform scientific knowledge into better agricultural outcomes. In some crops, such as sugarcane, an initially negative relationship could even be reversed when these factors reached high levels.
2-6-2026.p8: This finding has important implications for public policies. For years it has been assumed that increasing investment in agricultural research will be sufficient to increase food production. However, this study demonstrates that scientific evidence only generates benefits when an institutional environment capable of implementing it exists.
2-6-2026.p9: Research needs effective governments, solid institutions, resilient health systems, trained researchers, and adequate mechanisms to transfer knowledge to the productive sector. Without these elements, even a large scientific production can have a very limited impact on agriculture.
2-6-2026.p10: Ultimately, the main lesson is that scientific knowledge does not produce food on its own. What really determines its impact is the ability of each country to convert that knowledge into policies, innovation, and concrete actions in the field. That is probably the difference between publishing more research and ensuring that research truly transforms agricultural production.
2-6-2026.caption: Scientific coherence study published in Agriculture for crop production indicators.
2-6-2026.reference: Acosta-Monterrosa AA, Florián-Pérez MC, Montoya-Vega ME, Lozada-Martinez ID. Structural Capacity, Food Security-Related Publications, and Crop Production: A Multilevel Global Analysis Across Income Settings. Agriculture. 2026; 16(9):995.

2-7-2026.title: Is climate science where it's needed most? Scientific coherence to advance towards climate justice
2-7-2026.author: Andy A. Acosta-Monterrosa
2-7-2026.caption: Perspective and scientometric study published in Frontiers in Environmental Science on climate change.
2-7-2026.reference: Acosta-Monterrosa AA, Montoya-Quintero KF, Visconti-López FJ and Lozada-Martínez ID (2026) Scientific coherence in climate change research: a meta-research perspective to accelerate scientific progress and climate justice. Front. Environ. Sci. 14:1766738.
2-7-2026.p1: Climate change is one of the most urgent environmental challenges of our time. Its effects manifest in rising sea levels, biodiversity loss, and the increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, among other environmental, social, and economic consequences.
2-7-2026.p2: However, there is a profound paradox: those who have historically contributed most to climate change are not necessarily those who suffer its effects most intensely. While high-income countries have had a considerable share in cumulative greenhouse gas emissions, many of the most affected populations are found in low- and middle-income countries, where there are fewer resources to respond, adapt, and recover.
2-7-2026.p3: In this context, science has played a fundamental role. Through scientific articles, books, and reports, research has allowed us to understand the causes and consequences of climate change, as well as to develop mitigation and adaptation strategies. Therefore, scientific knowledge constitutes an essential pillar for decision-making at local, regional, and global levels.
2-7-2026.p4: Nevertheless, the rapid growth of climate research has not been distributed equitably. We have found that over 70% of the analyzed scientific production came from high- and upper-middle-income countries, highlighting a significant geographical concentration of knowledge.
2-7-2026.p5: This result raises fundamental questions: has the increase in publications translated into tangible improvements for the most affected populations and ecosystems? Is research concentrated in territories where climate vulnerability is greatest? Do the topics studied respond to real damages, local priorities, and adaptation needs?
2-7-2026.p6: To address these questions, from the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS) and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), we propose applying the concept of scientific coherence to climate change research.
2-7-2026.p7: Scientific coherence can be understood as the degree to which the volume and thematic, geographic, and temporal distribution of climate research correspond to the risk, vulnerability, and exposure patterns of populations and ecosystems. This approach helps identify whether the global scientific agenda responds to the most affected territories or if, conversely, it concentrates on less vulnerable contexts while other regions remain underrepresented.
2-7-2026.p8: To define the scope of this concept, we propose a framework composed of four pillars:
2-7-2026.p9: Geographic coherence. Evaluates whether research is produced in regions where climate risk and vulnerability are greatest, or whether researchers, institutions, and communities from those territories participate substantially in knowledge generation.
2-7-2026.p10: Thematic coherence. Examines whether the topics prioritized by research correspond to the problems and needs that matter most to affected populations and ecosystems, including local demands for adaptation, protection, and recovery.
2-7-2026.p11: Temporal coherence. Analyzes whether scientific production responds in a timely manner to emerging crises and critical moments of decision. Research can be relevant but lose utility if its results arrive too late to guide policies or prevent damages.
2-7-2026.p12: Translational coherence. Considers the extent to which the generated knowledge turns into public policies, local interventions, and concrete transformations that improve quality of life and help protect ecosystems.
2-7-2026.p13: The joint analysis of these dimensions allows us to go beyond the number of publications or citations received. It also helps to understand who produces the knowledge, what problems are prioritized, what populations participate in its construction, for whom the evidence is generated, and what concrete effects it has in the most affected territories.
2-7-2026.p14: Therefore, evaluating climate research solely based on its academic productivity can offer an incomplete view of its true contribution. It is also necessary to consider its social, territorial, and political relevance, as well as its capacity to respond to the inequalities that characterize both the impacts of climate change and knowledge production.
2-7-2026.p15: Advancing towards coherent climate science requires strengthening the participation of researchers, institutions, and communities from the most vulnerable regions, promoting more equitable international collaborations, and directing resources towards questions relevant to local contexts. Likewise, it involves facilitating the translation of scientific results into policies, adaptation actions, and concrete interventions.
2-7-2026.p16: On a rapidly warming planet, scientific progress should not be measured solely by the amount of knowledge produced, but also by its capacity to respond to the most urgent risks, reduce inequalities, and support decisions that protect people and ecosystems. Scientific coherence can help close the gap between academic production and the real needs of territories, accelerating both scientific progress and climate justice.

2-8-2026.title: How do we know which treatment works if every study defines intestinal failure differently?
2-8-2026.author: Fabriccio J. Visconti-Lopez
2-8-2026.caption: Systematic review and meta-research study published in BMC Gastroenterology on intestinal failure.
2-8-2026.reference: Montoya-Quintero KF, Valencia S, Pérez MCF, Visconti-Lopez FJ, Marín-Hamburguer Y, Lozada-Martinez ID. Conceptual and operational consistency in defining intestinal failure across randomized controlled trials: a systematic review and meta-research analysis. BMC Gastroenterol. 2026 Jan 21;26(1):128.
2-8-2026.p1: Clinical trials allow us to know if a treatment works and if its benefits outweigh its risks. However, before comparing treatments, it is necessary to answer a basic question: are all studies really investigating the same disease?
2-8-2026.p2: This question is especially important in intestinal failure, a rare but serious condition. It occurs when the intestine loses the ability to absorb enough nutrients, water, and mineral salts to maintain health or growth. As a consequence, some people need to receive fluids or nutrients directly through a vein.
2-8-2026.p3: Although there are international definitions to identify this condition, their application in clinical trials has not always been uniform. Some studies consider the need for intravenous support. Others use intestine length, stool volume, or the diagnosis of short bowel syndrome. These criteria describe related aspects, but do not necessarily identify the same group of patients.
2-8-2026.p4: To study this problem, a team of researchers from Colombia (Universidad de la Costa, Universidad de Caldas) and Peru (Universidad Científica del Sur), with the participation of researchers linked to the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS), and its Center for Meta-Science and Scientometrics in Biomedical Sciences (METRIC-BIO), conducted a systematic review and meta-research analysis. The objective was to examine how clinical trials defined intestinal failure and determine whether those definitions matched international criteria.
2-8-2026.p5: Researchers reviewed 9,354 scientific records and ultimately included 12 clinical trials published between 2011 and 2025. Together, these studies gathered 617 participants. Most were conducted in high-income countries and studied adults, although some trials included a pediatric population. The main finding was clear: only three of the 12 trials, equivalent to 25%, presented an explicit definition of intestinal failure aligned with the recommendations of the European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism.
2-8-2026.p6: The majority used practical criteria to select their participants. For example, some studies required people to receive intravenous support at least three days a week for 12 months. Four trials incorporated indirect indicators, such as producing more than 1,500 grams of stool per day or having a certain intestinal length. Two studies used the term intestinal failure without explaining how the diagnosis was established.
2-8-2026.p7: The problem is not that these criteria lack utility. The frequency of intravenous support or stool volume can help identify people with severe intestinal disorders. However, none of these elements should be used in isolation to replace a complete definition of the disease.
2-8-2026.p8: To illustrate, a person may have short bowel syndrome and retain enough absorptive capacity to not depend on intravenous support. Another may require it due to a functional alteration, even if they have a longer intestinal length. If both profiles are classified in the same way, trials could end up evaluating treatments in clinically different populations.
2-8-2026.p9: This variability has consequences. When studies include patients with different characteristics under the same diagnosis, it is more difficult to compare their results. It also increases uncertainty when combining multiple studies in a systematic review, formulating clinical recommendations, or deciding which patients might benefit from a treatment.
2-8-2026.p10: The problem persisted even in recent research. Explicit definitions were absent in trials published before 2017 and only appeared in three of the nine subsequent studies. This indicates that the publication of international consensus has not guaranteed their systematic incorporation into the design of clinical trials.
2-8-2026.p11: The authors propose that future trials should indicate a minimum of three elements. First, which international definition they used. Second, what type of intestinal failure the participants present. Third, what practical criteria, such as the duration and frequency of intravenous support, were employed to confirm the diagnosis.
2-8-2026.p12: Defining a disease may seem like a matter of words. In reality, it determines who participates in studies, to whom their results apply, and what healthcare decisions are made. Useful science for patients begins with making sure everyone is talking about the same condition.

2-9-2026.title: What does it mean to be among the most cited researchers in the world? An international recognition of Colombian science
2-9-2026.author: Andy A. Acosta-Monterrosa
2-9-2026.subtitle: Dr. Iván David Lozada-Martínez is ranked in the global Top 2% Scientists according to Stanford University and Scopus.
2-9-2026.caption: Dr. Iván David Lozada-Martínez, MD, MSc, Founder & CEO of CECIMIB SAS. CECIMIB Archives.
2-9-2026.secondaryImageCaption: Infographic: Summary of the ranking and distribution of Dr. Iván David Lozada-Martínez in the global Top 2% Scientists ranking (Ioannidis et al., 2026).
2-9-2026.reference: Ioannidis JPA. August 2026 data-update for “Updated science-wide author databases of standardized citation indicators”. Elsevier Data Repository. 2026; Version 9.
2-9-2026.p1: Every year, thousands of researchers around the world dedicate their efforts to producing new knowledge, answering scientific questions, and contributing to the advancement of their disciplines. Their work is published in specialized journals, shared at conferences, and, in many cases, serves as the starting point for new investigations.
2-9-2026.p2: However, an important question arises: how can we identify which researchers have achieved greater visibility and impact within the international scientific community?
2-9-2026.p3: One of the best-known tools to approach this question is the global database of highly cited researchers developed by John P. A. Ioannidis, a researcher at Stanford University, along with Kevin W. Boyack and Jeroen Baas. This initiative, internationally known as the Top 2% Scientists, uses Scopus data to identify researchers whose work demonstrates outstanding citation impact indicators.
2-9-2026.p4: In its ninth version, released in October 2026 with citation data corresponding to the year 2025, this database included Colombian physician and researcher Iván David Lozada-Martínez, MD, MSc, founder and CEO of the Center for Scientific Consulting and Meta-Research in Biomedical Sciences (CECIMIB SAS).
2-9-2026.p5: This recognition is particularly noteworthy when examining his standing within the field of surgery. According to the reported results, Dr. Lozada-Martínez ranked 2,070th among 146,713 profiles evaluated in the Surgery subfield, placing him in the top 1.41% worldwide. Furthermore, he is among only four Colombian researchers included in this specific category and is the sole researcher affiliated with the Universidad de la Costa (CUC) appearing in this subfield.
2-9-2026.p6: But what does it really mean to be part of this database?
2-9-2026.p7: Unlike other rankings that primarily focus on the sheer number of published papers, the methodology developed by Ioannidis and collaborators utilizes a composite indicator called the c-score. This metric integrates six bibliometric indicators, including total citations received, the h-index, a co-authorship-adjusted index, and citations obtained based on the researcher's position as single, first, or last author of a publication.
2-9-2026.p8: In simple terms, it is not merely about tallying how many studies an individual has published, but examining how their contributions have been utilized and cited by peers. For instance, when a scientific paper is cited in a new study, it indicates that the work has been incorporated as a foundation within subsequent research. The accumulation of these academic connections helps map the scholarly influence of published knowledge.
2-9-2026.p9: Nevertheless, it is crucial to recognize that citations do not serve as an absolute measure of scientific quality. A higher number of citations does not necessarily prove that a study is methodologically superior, nor does it inherently establish clinical or social impact. Therefore, this ranking should be understood as a bibliometric assessment tool rather than a definitive appraisal of a researcher's overall excellence.
2-9-2026.p10: This distinction holds particular significance for CECIMIB, whose scientific agenda focuses on meta-research, scientometrics, and the critical appraisal of biomedical evidence. These disciplines seek to understand not only how much knowledge the scientific community produces, but also how it is generated, how it is utilized, and how reliable the evaluation methods are.
2-9-2026.p11: Dr. Lozada-Martínez's inclusion in this database represents an important milestone in his academic career and highlights the international visibility achieved by his scientific contributions. Likewise, it serves as a source of institutional pride for CECIMIB, illustrating the active engagement of Colombian researchers within international networks of knowledge production and dissemination.
2-9-2026.p12: In a landscape where scientific research continually faces challenges in funding, collaboration, and institutional support, these results also prompt reflection on the importance of fostering conditions that nurture sustainable scientific careers.
2-9-2026.p13: Because the true value of science lies not merely in attaining distinguished positions within a ranking, but in generating rigorous, reliable, and meaningful knowledge capable of advancing research and improving societal well-being.
2-9-2026.p14: From CECIMIB, we congratulate Dr. Iván David Lozada-Martínez on this international recognition and reaffirm our dedication to strengthening biomedical research, meta-science, and evidence-based scientific evaluation.
